title: How Wars in the Middle East and Europe Are Reshaping the Way Indians Travel Abroad
excerpt: Rerouted flights, surging airfares, and drone disruptions are turning Indian travelers into strategic planners who prioritize flexibility over destination.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Airlines have rerouted India-to-Europe flights, increasing fares by 25-35%.
  • Indian travelers are now strategic, booking last-minute and prioritizing flexibility.
  • Domestic tourism is booming, with hotel occupancy up 5% year-over-year.
  • Southeast Asia is gaining popularity among cost-conscious Indian travelers.

  • Conflicts in the Middle East and Europe have forced airlines to reroute India-to-Europe flights, adding hours of flying time and pushing fares up 25-35% on popular routes.
  • Indian travelers are not canceling trips but are becoming "strategic travelers" — booking later, choosing flexible tickets, and carrying backup plans.
  • Domestic tourism is surging as a result, with hotel occupancy up 5% and nearly half of all bookings now made within three days of travel.
  • Southeast Asian destinations like Thailand, Singapore, and Bali are gaining share from Europe and the Middle East among cost-conscious Indian travelers.

Airspace Disruptions Force Flight Reroutes

The ongoing conflicts involving Iran and wider tensions across West Asia have closed off major air corridors between India and Europe, forcing airlines to chart longer routes that add hours to flying times and significant costs to fuel bills. For millions of Indians who travel internationally each year, the disruption has fundamentally changed the calculus of booking a holiday or a business trip.

Travel enthusiast Priyanka Sharangpani Joshi experienced this firsthand during a family trip to the UK and Russia. "A drone-related disruption at St Petersburg airport even forced us to consider changing our travel plans," she told Indian Express. "The experience made us realise that travel today is less about finding the perfect itinerary and more about being prepared for unexpected changes."

Marketing professional Akshat Chadha found Delhi-to-Phuket airfares had jumped 25-35% with fewer flight options available. "It was more difficult to find convenient schedules at reasonable prices," he said.

The Rise of the Strategic Traveler

Industry data tells a clear story: Indians have not stopped traveling, but they have changed how they travel. According to Wego, travelers are spending more time comparing fares, evaluating flight schedules, and monitoring geopolitical developments before committing to bookings.

"Rather than seeing widespread cancellations, travellers are spending more time comparing fares, evaluating flight schedules, and assessing their options before making a booking decision."

— Bernard Corraya, General Manager, Wego

Budget travel platform Zostel reports that nearly 48% of bookings now come in within three days of travel, with most remaining bookings made seven to ten days in advance. The last-minute booking pattern reflects a traveler base that wants to keep its options open until the geopolitical picture is clearer.

"Queries around real-time safety updates and travel advisories have also increased before bookings are confirmed, pointing to a traveller who is more informed and more cautious, but still travelling," said Aviral Gupta, CEO of Zostel.

Domestic Tourism Booms

Perhaps the most visible beneficiary of the global uncertainty is India's own tourism sector. Ravi Gosain, President of the Indian Association of Tour Operators, said there is clear evidence that travelers are shifting from international to domestic destinations. India recorded an estimated 303 crore domestic trips in 2025 and welcomed over 20 million international tourists including NRIs in the same year.

Radisson Hotel Group reports that overall occupancy across its India portfolio has increased by 5% year-over-year, with leisure destination properties approaching 75% average occupancy. Destinations combining recreation, spirituality, and nature — Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Goa, Rajasthan, Kerala — are seeing the strongest gains.

Spiritual tourism has proven particularly resilient. Ayodhya, Varanasi, Prayagraj, and Rishikesh continue to draw large volumes despite — or perhaps because of — the uncertainties plaguing international travel.

What NRI Travelers Should Know

For NRIs planning trips to India or routing through the Middle East, the disruptions carry practical implications. Flights between India and Europe that once crossed Iranian and Pakistani airspace are now taking longer routes over Central Asia or further south, adding one to three hours of travel time.

Srijit Nair of Rail Europe noted that Indian travelers visiting Europe are increasingly opting for rail travel between cities rather than booking multiple short-haul flights. "Value, flexibility, and confidence are becoming just as important as the destination itself," he said.

Adventure traveler Gurpreet Dhindsa, who recently traveled to Kabul, found the impact on less-traveled routes even more pronounced. "Commercial carriers are having to avoid unstable airspace, including parts of Iran and restricted zones along the India-Pakistan border. This has significantly affected route planning."

Where Indians Are Heading Instead

While Europe remains aspirational, the practical shift in demand favors closer destinations. Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, Japan, Bali, and Sri Lanka are all seeing robust demand thanks to proximity, strong air connectivity, and appeal across a range of budgets.

The hotel industry is adapting with dynamic pricing, flexible cancellation policies, staycation packages, and stronger digital engagement. K B Kachru, President of the Hotel Association of India, acknowledged that some hotels had seen a near-term drop in overseas bookings, but said India's domestic tourism base has cushioned the sector.

For now, the message from India's travel industry is cautiously optimistic: Indians will keep traveling, but the age of the impulsive international booking appears to be over. The "strategic traveler" is here to stay.
